lead.t: Pre-conception care is a set of interventions that identify and modify biomedical, behavioural and social risks to a woman's health and to future pregnancies.

snip.t: Pre-conception care is a set of interventions that identify and modify biomedical, behavioural and social risks to a woman's health and to future pregnancies.

faq.a: It reduces neural‑tube defects; the neural tube closes by week 4, often before pregnancy is known.
faq.q: Why is folic acid given before pregnancy?

faq.a: Yes, if viral load is suppressed with ART and appropriate intrapartum prophylaxis are used.
faq.q: Can a woman with HIV have a healthy baby?

faq.a: Identify cause (iron, folate, chronic disease) and start iron/folic acid while investigating further.
faq.q: What is the first step if anemia is found?

exam: What investigations would you order for a woman planning pregnancy who has a BMI of 32? — Assess anemia, diabetes, HIV, hepatitis B, blood pressure; BMI >30 signals need for glucose tolerance test and nutrition counselling.

A 28‑year‑old with sickle cell disease wants to conceive. How do you manage her pre‑conception? — Optimize hemoglobin, vaccinate, give folic acid, discuss hydroxyurea cessation, arrange specialist obstetric review.
Why is ACE inhibitor therapy contraindicated in pre‑conception care? — It causes fetal renal dysgenesis and skull hypoplasia; switch to labetalol or methyldopa.
How would you counsel a woman using khat daily about pregnancy risk? — Explain cardiovascular stress, possible fetal growth restriction, and offer cessation support.

You find a positive rapid syphilis test in a woman planning pregnancy, but the confirmatory test is unavailable. What do you do? — Treat presumptively with benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM weekly for 3 weeks; inform partner and arrange follow‑up.
What red‑flag symptom in a pre‑conception visit requires urgent referral? — New onset chest pain or dyspnoea suggesting cardiac disease; refer immediately.

Explain the difference between pre‑conception care and antenatal care in exam answer form. — Pre‑conception focuses on risk modification before conception; antenatal care monitors pregnancy progress and fetal wellbeing after conception.

A woman with uncontrolled hypertension presents for pre‑conception counselling. What is your next step? — Initiate safe antihypertensive (labetalol or methyldopa), aim for BP <140/90 mmHg, and defer pregnancy until control achieved.

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Pre‑conception care identifies and modifies biomedical, behavioural and social risks before pregnancy, improving maternal and fetal outcomes. In low‑resource settings it focuses on common infections, nutrition, and access to safe contraception.

b: Screen for chronic disease, infections, medication teratogenicity, nutritional deficiencies, and psychosocial factors.
Use a checklist (medical history, physical exam, labs, vaccination status, lifestyle review).
sections.p: A structured set of interventions delivered to women of reproductive age before conception to assess and optimise health, reduce modifiable risks and plan for a safe pregnancy.

b: Low: no chronic disease, normal BMI, up‑to‑date immunisations.
Moderate: single controlled chronic condition, mild anaemia, BMI 25‑29.
High: uncontrolled diabetes, HIV with high viral load, sickle cell disease, severe anaemia, active TB.
sections.p: Risk is stratified as low, moderate or high based on the number and seriousness of identified problems.

b: Biomedical: untreated hypertension, diabetes, anemia, HIV, hepatitis B, sickle cell, schistosomiasis.
Behavioural: tobacco, alcohol, khat, unsafe sex, poor diet, lack of folic acid.
Social: low education, gender‑based violence, limited access to health services.
sections.p: Risks fall into three categories: biomedical, behavioural and social.

b: Unplanned pregnancy, recurrent miscarriage, or previous obstetric complications raise suspicion of unmet pre‑conception needs.
sections.p: Women may be asymptomatic; the ‘presentation’ is the identification of risk factors during routine visits or family‑planning encounters.
When a test is unavailable, use clinical proxies (e.g., pallor for anemia, capillary glucose for diabetes) and refer for higher‑level care if needed.

t.b: Detect anemia, infection or thrombocytopenia; anemia <11 g/dL warrants iron/folate therapy.
Identify pre‑diabetes/diabetes; HbA1c ≥6.5 % requires optimisation before conception.

t.a: Serology for HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis
t.b: Screen for transmissible infections; positive HIV → start ART, hepatitis B → vaccinate partner, consider antiviral prophylaxis.
Detect asymptomatic bacteriuria; treat with nitrofurantoin if pregnancy likely.
Assess iron stores; <15 µg/L indicates iron deficiency needing supplementation.
Identify hypertension; >140/90 mmHg requires control before conception.
Detect hypothyroidism; TSH >4.0 mIU/L warrants levothyroxine.
Low levels guide high‑dose folic acid prescription.

b: Severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL) → cardiac failure.
Uncontrolled HIV (viral load >1000 copies/mL) → vertical transmission.
Active TB or malaria → miscarriage, low birth weight.
Uncorrected uterine anomalies → recurrent miscarriage.
sections.p: Uncontrolled high‑risk conditions can cause maternal mortality, fetal loss, or congenital anomalies.

b: Start or optimise ART for HIV; aim for viral suppression.
Treat malaria prophylactically in endemic areas; give intermittent preventive therapy.
Control hypertension with labetalol or methyldopa (avoid ACE inhibitors).
Counsell on smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, safe sex, and nutrition.
Vaccinate against rubella, hepatitis B, tetanus if non‑immune.
sections.p: Address each risk with evidence‑based, low‑cost interventions; prioritize treatable conditions before conception.

b: Repeat hemoglobin, blood pressure and infection screens.
Document contraception use and timing of planned pregnancy.
Educate on early antenatal booking.
sections.p: Re‑assess risk after 3‑6 months or sooner if a condition changes. Provide a written pre‑conception plan and refer to specialist care when high risk persists.

b: Antenatal care: monitoring fetal growth, not risk modification before conception.
Family‑planning counselling: may include pre‑conception advice but not full risk assessment.
sections.p: Pre‑conception care is distinct from antenatal care (which begins after conception) and from post‑abortion care (which focuses on immediate recovery).

b: Serum ferritin can be normal in inflammation despite iron deficiency; consider CRP.
Rapid HIV tests have a window period; repeat if recent exposure suspected.
Urine dipstick may miss low‑grade bacteriuria; culture is preferred.
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal in early disease or in low‑resource settings.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypertension (>160/110 mmHg), chest pain, dyspnoea, or syncope.
